A midget, historically, referred to a human being who is very small in height, but whose body is proportionally normal — meaning all body parts (arms, legs, torso, head) are small but shaped and sized in the same ratio as an average person's body. Think of it like a scaled-down version of a typical human body.

To truly understand "midget," you need to understand what it was contrasted with — the word dwarf.

These two words were historically used to describe two different kinds of short stature:

Dwarf referred to a person of very small height whose body is disproportionate — meaning some parts of the body did not shrink equally. Most commonly, a dwarf would have a normal-sized torso and head but significantly shorter arms and legs. This is typically caused by a medical condition called achondroplasia, which affects how bones and cartilage develop.

Midget, on the other hand, described a person whose entire body was uniformly small — every part shrank together in proportion. The medical term for this is proportionate dwarfism, and it can result from a deficiency of growth hormone or other rare conditions.

So the historical difference was simple:

  • Dwarf = small height, uneven body proportions
  • Midget = small height, even body proportions
The Big Problem: Why This Word Is Offensive Today

Even though "midget" once had a specific technical meaning, it is now considered highly offensive, disrespectful, and hurtful by the vast majority of people with short stature, medical professionals, and disability advocates.

Here is why:

1. It has a painful history of mockery.
The word became strongly associated with circus and sideshow entertainment in the 19th and early 20th centuries, where people of very small stature were publicly displayed for entertainment and profit — often mocked or treated as oddities. Because of this, the word carries a deeply dehumanizing history.

2. It reduces people to a physical trait.
Calling a person a "midget" defines them entirely by their height, stripping away their full humanity and individuality.

3. The medical community has moved away from it.
Doctors and healthcare professionals no longer use "midget" as a clinical term. It has no place in modern medical language.

4. People who are short in stature find it deeply hurtful.
Organizations like Little People of America (LPA) actively campaign against the use of this word and have formally stated that it is a slur.

The respectful, accepted terms are:

  • Little person (most preferred)
  • Person with dwarfism
  • Person of short stature

These terms respect the individual's full humanity while acknowledging their physical characteristic only when it is relevant.
Is It Ever Used in Other Ways?

Yes. As an adjective (not a noun), "midget" is sometimes still used informally to describe a very small version of something non-human — for example, "a midget car" or "midget golf" (what many people call mini-golf). Some sports leagues for young children are also called "midget leagues." These non-human uses are separate from the noun usage and are gradually being replaced by words like "mini," "miniature," or "junior."

The noun form almost always refers to a person — and in that form, it is considered a slur and should not be used.

As a noun, "midget" was once used to describe a person of unusually small height whose body proportions were normal throughout. It was technically distinguished from "dwarf," which described someone with disproportionate body features. However, the word is now widely recognized as offensive and harmful due to its history of use in ridicule and dehumanization. It should not be used to refer to any person. The respectful modern alternatives are "little person" or "person with dwarfism."
